cells.tense: The collapse has already happened, and the ground in front of you is open, and you are standing on your own feet on it.
cells.ask: Name one thing the cleared ground is now free for, out loud to someone — so the tending gets seen, not just done.
cells.core:
This is you with both hands in the open ground, one row going in while you keep an eye on the other, and neither one starving. What fell down fell because it couldn't hold, and you're not trying to build it back — you're working the space it left, planting what survives a real season. It's slow work and it's holding. You know which of the two demands can wait and which can't, and you move between them without a lot of noise.

The tending doesn't have to stay invisible. Let someone see the hands in it and hear what it cost — that's how the work finishes in you, not just in the ground.
cells.sheetLine: You're tending what's still standing, on ground you didn't have before.
cells.verb: tending what's growing with steady hands, both demands held, neither dropped
cells.place: in the clearing where what couldn't stand has just come down and the ground is finally level

cells.tense: You're standing on the new ground already planning the harvest, and the season you're describing hasn't arrived yet.
cells.ask: Pick one thing that's actually here today and give it your hands — the rest can wait for a season that's actually landed.
cells.core:
In its good hour this is you at the edge of the clearing with a watering can and one plant, patient, unhurried, because you've already lived through enough to trust the timeline. You tend what's in front of you and let the rest keep its own schedule. That's care that isn't exhausted — hands on the actual thing, not on the idea of it.

What you're doing now is caretaking a future version of this. The cleared ground isn't even settled and you've mapped what should grow on every inch, what it means if it doesn't, what you'll do about it. The tending has jumped ahead of the growing. Care that doesn't exhaust stays with what's in front of it, and what's in front of you is smaller than the plan. Let it be that size for a while.
cells.sheetLine: You're tending a harvest that hasn't been planted yet.
cells.verb: tending what's growing with steady hands, both demands held, neither dropped

cells.tense: The ground opened up and you're still standing at the old structure, watching it come down from where you were.
cells.ask: Put your hands on one small living thing — the next right tending, at the size it actually is — and let it grow you back into the clearing.
cells.core:
In its good hour this is you out in the open with dirt on your hands, one thing at a time, unhurried. You'd know which small thing needed you today and you'd give it that much and no more. Steady, undramatic, alive.

Right now something fell and you're not out on the new ground. You can see the clearing — it's right there — but you're standing where the walls were, watching the space like it belongs to someone else. The tending stopped and hasn't picked back up. What brings you forward isn't a bigger push. It's one small thing that answers when you show up. Keep showing up to it, and the growing pulls you out into the open with it.
cells.sheetLine: The clearing is here and you're still standing where the old walls were.
cells.verb: tending what's growing with steady hands, both demands held, neither dropped
cells.place: in the clearing where what couldn't stand has just come down and the ground is finally level

cells.tense: You're already out on the new ground, tending what's there, and you're talking about it like it's just what needed doing.
cells.ask: Say out loud that you're the one who kept this alive through the collapse — just once, to one person, in your own words.
cells.core:
In its good hour this is you knowing exactly whose hands these are. You tend the open ground, you say what it's costing, and you let the people around you see the work as yours. That's the finished shape — care that's visible, rest that follows, nothing carried in the dark.

What's happening is you've been keeping things alive through all of this and calling it just what had to happen. The careful holding, the two demands you never dropped, the slow work nobody asked about — it's real and it's yours. There's a moment when holding on turns into letting go, and you don't reach it by carrying quietly forever. Name what you carried. The naming is how the carrying finishes.
cells.sheetLine: You kept this alive and you're calling it nothing.
